Working Paper Series 
When less is more: behavioral effects 
of CBDC holding limits 
 
Thomas Garcia, Claudia Lambert, 
Cosimo Pancaro, Claire Rimbaud, Alice Soldà

No 3300 / October 2026 

Abstract
Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies
(CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance,
they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted
an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously
varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects
from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of
payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect. This effect is material
only when the limit is high enough. Enabling reverse waterfall —automatic conversion into this
limited means of payment— increases adoption while reducing holdings. These results suggest
that combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms can support CBDC use while
containing holdings, thereby helping to mitigate potential financial stability risks.
Keywords: CBDC, holding limits, digital currency, behavioral economics, experimental economics.
JEL codes: E42, C91, D14, E58.

Non-technical summary
Several central banks are exploring the possibility of issuing a central bank digital currency (CBDC)
— a digital form of public money for everyday payments. The CBDC design needs to balance ease of
use with ensuring that it preserves financial stability. In response, most CBDC projects foresee the
introduction of a holding limit, which would cap the amount of CBDC that individuals could hold in
their digital wallets. At the same time, automatic funding mechanisms such as the reverse waterfall
functionality can allow individuals to make payments even when they do not hold sufficient CBDC,
potentially reducing the need to hold large CBDC balances.
While holding limits would mechanically restrict how much CBDC people can hold, they may also
have a behavioral impact. For example, some individuals may view the limit as a restriction of their
decision rights, decreasing the attractiveness of the CBDC. For others, instead, the limit can act as a
reference point, attracting CBDC holdings towards that value. Understanding these possible responses
is important to assess how much CBDC people would actually hold and thus anticipate its impact on
the financial system if such limits were introduced.
This paper investigates how holding limits influence individuals’ choices about how to allocate their
money between different payment instruments. In particular, it studies whether the introduction of
a limit changes individuals’ behavior beyond its direct mechanical effect. The analysis also provides
empirical evidence on the reverse waterfall functionality. This mechanism automatically converts funds
from a user’s commercial bank account into CBDC whenever the user needs to make a payment but
does not currently hold enough CBDC.
To disentangle the direct effect of the limit from its behavioral effects, the paper uses a controlled
online experiment with 761 participants from four euro area countries: France, Germany, Italy, and
Spain. In the experiment, participants made decisions about how to allocate tokens between two
means of payment, then faced automated sellers, and earned money if they held the means of payment
required by the seller. One instrument bears interest but is not always accepted, while the other pays
no interest, is always accepted for payments and could be subject to a holding limit. These differences
capture the essence of the differences between bank-card payment and CBDC, where the former can
be remunerated via a deposit account and the latter can be used for peer-to-peer payments. Our

identification strategy relies on comparing participants’ decisions in the absence and the presence of
a limit, and assessing whether the level of the limit affects these behavioral responses by comparing
decisions with relatively lower and higher limits. In addition, we investigate how the presence of a
reverse waterfall functionality affects individuals’ responses to these limits.
Our results show that holding limits can generate indirect behavioral effects. Participants whose
initial holdings are below the limit, and thus would be expected to keep the same allocation in the
absence of indirect effects, tend on average to increase their holdings when the limit is introduced.
Moreover, distinguishing between relatively lower and higher limits, we find that this increase in
holdings emerges only when the limit is higher due to an asymmetric impact of attraction and repulsion.
When the limit is lower, the opposing behavioral responses offset each other, leaving average holdings
unchanged. By contrast, when the limit is set at a higher level, the anchoring effect becomes stronger
while the negative reaction to the restriction becomes weaker. As a result, average holdings increase
after the limit is introduced with the higher limit.
Finally, we find that introducing a reverse waterfall functionality both increases adoption of the
limited means of payment and decreases the level of its holdings. This suggests that these kind
of automated funding mechanisms can allow individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of
CBDC without requiring them to hold large CBDC balances.
Overall, we provide the first evidence that combining holding limits with automatic funding mech-
anisms can support the use of CBDC as a means of payment while addressing concerns about potential
financial stability risks.

1 Introduction
Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC) are digital forms of sovereign currency issued by the central
bank. Several central banks are currently designing retail CBDC to complement physical cash by
providing individuals with an additional state-backed means of payment (Illes et al., 2025). CBDC
would bring central bank money into the digital age aiming to support financial inclusion, protect
privacy, and make payments easier and more secure for all. They would complement banknotes and
coins, giving people an additional choice about how to pay. However, preventing users from storing
excessive amounts in CBDC is also important to avoid excessive outflows of deposits from banks,
preserving financial stability. To address this concern, central banks such as the ECB, the Bank of
England, the Bank of Canada or the People’s Bank of China are designing CBDC that would feature
a “holding limit” which would limit, at any point in time, the amount of CBDC that individuals
could hold in their digital wallet (Panetta, 2022; Demertzis and Mejino-L´ op
ez, 2024).1 In parallel,
several CBDC projects are considering automatic funding mechanisms which would allow users to
make payments in CBDC without maintaining large CBDC balances.
Motivated by this central feature of CBDC, this paper studies how imposing a holding limit on
a means of payment affects consumers’ liquid wealth allocation. Introducing a holding limit has an
obvious direct effect on individuals’ allocation decisions by preventing users from exceeding the limit.
In addition to this mechanical effect, holding limits can have indirect behavioral effects reflecting a
change in consumer attitudes toward the means of payment that can further affect holdings. The
direction of these indirect effects is a priori not clear. On the one hand, users may perceive a means
of payment associated with a holding limit as a less attractive solution, leading them to hold fewer
funds in CBDC than what is directly implied by the mechanical impact. Indeed, a limit can have an
aversive impact by reducing decision rights (e.g. Bartling et al., 2014). On the other hand, the holding
limit can act as a reference or anchoring point when individuals choose how much to hold, potentially
leading them to hold amounts close to the limit, whereas they might have held less otherwise (e.g.
Ariely et al., 2003; Abeler et al., 2011).2 Given that these effects are behavioral and real-world data
on CBDC holdings are unavailable due to the lack of a large-scale CBDC implementation, we use an

cognitive heuristics.

experimental approach to assess whether indirect effects occur and, if so, to identify the direction of
their influence on holdings.
Despite the importance of understanding the impact of a holding limit on CBDC holdings, to date,
there is no paper explicitly dedicated to this question. Incentivized experiments on CBDC have focused
on different aspects of the introduction of a CBDC on individuals’ portfolio allocations including the
introduction of a new payment method (Arifovic et al., 2023), greater privacy compared with other
digital payment instruments (Borgonovo et al., 2021; Magin et al., 2026), the possibility of bearing
interest (Camera, 2024), and their digital nature relative to cash (Camera et al., 2016).3 However, they
do not address the role of the holding limit. 4 More closely related to our contribution, some studies
use surveys, which include questions on holding limits but do not experimentally manipulate either
the existence or the level of such limits. For example, van der Horst and van Gent (2025) conduct
a survey experiment on digital euro and find that, on average, participants consider e1,297 to be a
logical amount for a holding limit by directly asking for the amounts to participants. Bidder et al.
(2024) develop a quantitative macroeconomic model calibrated using survey data and show that the
introduction of a holding limit is a necessary condition for a CBDC to be welfare-improving. Even
closer to our study, Georgarakos et al. (2025) estimate in a survey experiment the causal effect of
holding limits ranging from e1000 to e120000 on the propensity to adopt the digital euro and the
amount allocated to it compared with other liquid assets. They find that higher holding limits tend
to increase amount allocated.
Our preregistered study contributes to the literature by causally assessing the overall impact of
the introduction of a holding limit on individuals’ portfolio allocation while disentangling its direct
mechanical effect from its indirect behavioral effects. To achieve this objective, we employ an online
incentivized experiment that exogenously varies both the presence and the level of a holding limit.
Specifically, participants face an allocation decision between two means of payment, first without any
holding limit, and subsequently with one means subject to a holding limit. The baseline (No Limit )
condition allows us to elicit individual behavior in the absence of constraints, which can then be
compared to the behavior under the imposition of a holding limit to identify causal effects. After the

allocation choice, participants use allocated tokens in trading activities that generate monetary payoffs.
Our experimental design differentiates itself from previous survey-based experiments by incorporating
real monetary incentives, thereby mitigating potential biases commonly found in survey studies (e.g.,
social desirability bias, hypothetical bias, etc.; Camerer and Hogarth , 1999).
In addition, we investigate how the presence of a reverse waterfall functionality affects individuals’
responses to these limits. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study how individuals
respond to a CBDC associated with a reverse waterfall (R W) functionality, a key feature designed
to preserve CBDC usability while limiting holdings in, for example, the foreseen design of the digital
euro (ECB, 2024b).5 This functionality enables users to draw on funds from a linked commercial
bank deposit account automatically converting them into CBDC whenever the user’s CBDC balance
is insufficient to complete a payment. This functionality is designed to operate alongside holding limits,
allowing policymakers to constrain CBDC holdings without restricting the use of CBDC as a means of
payment. However, little is known empirically about how individuals would respond to such a feature
or about its effect on CBDC holdings. To address this gap, our experimental design includes a final
condition in which the reverse waterfall functionality is enabled in the presence of a holding limit.
Our subject pool consists of 761 individuals from the four most populous euro area countries—
France, Germany, Italy, and Spain—, all recruited via the online research platform Prolific. Sampling
potential future users of the digital euro across multiple countries enhances the external validity of our
findings for the euro area. 6
Our results highlight that holding limits can generate indirect behavioral effects, beyond their
mechanical role of capping maximum holdings. We find evidence of two opposing mechanisms affecting
the holdings of a substantial fraction of “unconstrained” individuals (i.e., those whose initial CBDC
holdings were below the limit). About 37% of them either increase (“attraction effect”) or decrease
(“repulsion effect”) their CBDC holdings once the limit is introduced and these effects cannot be
attributed to the mechanical impact of the limit. The overall net change thus depends on the relative
strength of each indirect effect, which appears to depend on the level at which the limit is set. Under the

lower limit, attraction and repulsion offset each other, leaving the average holdings of the unconstrained
individuals unaffected. Under the higher limit, the repulsion effect is attenuated while the attraction
effect is strengthened, leading to a net increase in holdings of the limited means of payment among
unconstrained participants. Strikingly, when the limit is relatively high, the indirect behavioral effect
dominates the direct mechanical effect, resulting in higher average holdings of the limited means of
payment in the whole sample.
Finally, we show that introducing a reverse waterfall functionality increases adoption while reducing
average holdings. Thus, the waterfall can allow individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of
CBDC without requiring them to hold large CBDC balances. Taken together, these results highlight
the potential value of combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms to support CBDC
use while containing CBDC holdings.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: section 2 presents the experimental design,
section 3 reports the theoretical framework and hypotheses, section 4 presents the results and section 5
concludes.
2 Experimental Design
In our experiment, participants first allocate their tokens between two means of payment, then they
face automated sellers with whom they aim to complete trades. One means of payment, bank-card,
yields interests but is rejected by some sellers while the other one, CBDC, is universally accepted but
non-remunerated.7 The experiment follows a 3 × 2 design varying the presence of a limit and its level.
2.1 Characteristics of the means of payment
The characteristics of the two payment methods draw inspiration from key features of bank-card and
CBDC payments. However, they are not intended to replicate these payment methods in full detail,
but to introduce stylized comparative advantages to capture their essential characteristics while main-
taining a simplified structure that facilitates the understanding of the participants. Tokens allocated

2.2 Stages, treatments and conditions
The experiment is composed of three conditions and two treatments. Each condition consists of two
stages: an allocation stage and a trading stage.
Allocation stage: Participants face an allocation decision in which they need to allocate their
endowment of 10 tokens between the two payment methods.
Trading stage: After their allocation decision, participants face 10 sellers with whom they can
“trade” in 10 successive rounds. Participants are incentivized to realize successful trades. 11 Require-
ments needed for a trade to be successful are varied between conditions.
Condition variations: As mentioned earlier, each participant faces three conditions during the
experiment (see Figure 1). In the No Limit condition, there is no limit on the number of tokens they
can allocate to their bank-card holdings. In the Limit and Limit & R W conditions, the number of
tokens that can be allocated to CBDC holdings is capped (the ceiling is varied between treatments).
In addition, the Limit & R W condition differs from the other two as regards the outcome of a trade
with a seller accepting only CBDC if the participant does not have tokens allocated to CBDC when
meeting the seller. In the No Limit and Limit, this trade fails. By contrast, in the Limit & R W
condition a token is automatically transferred from bank to CBDC holdings and is used to complete
the trade, providing that the participant has allocated at least one token to CBDC holdings in the
allocation phase. This latter constraint captures the need to have a CBDC account open to use the
reverse waterfall mechanism.
Treatment variations: There are two treatments, which are varied randomly at the subject level.
Each participant faces either a limit of 3 (Low Limit ) or of 8 (High Limit ) tokens in the Limit and
Limit & R W conditions.

2.3 Experimen
tal procedures
The experiment was conducted online using the platform Prolific in November 2025. A total of 761
individuals participated from the four most populated euro area countries, namely France, Germany,
Italy, and Spain (190 participants per country except 191 for Spain; 374 in the Low Limit treatment
and 387 in the High Limit treatment). Instructions were provided in the native language of each
country (see English translation in Appendix E). The average age of the participants was 35 years old
(sd = 11) and 49.6% were female.
One condition, among the 3 conditions, was randomly selected for the payment. Each successful
trade yielded 10 points and points were converted at a rate of 50 points per £1.12 The bonus payment
was on average equal to £1.98. It adds to the hourly average payment of £2 (median time of 13
minutes) to constitute the total payoff per subject.
All participants faced the conditions in the same order: No Limit, Limit and Limit & R W. We
chose to position the No Limit condition first in order to have a benchmark allocation where the
potential implementation of a limit was unknown to the subject. Indeed, withdrawing the limit could
have affected allocations in a No Limit condition presented second thus preventing a clean estimation
of the impact of introducing a limit. Although this choice may introduce a potential order effect,
the design leaves little room for such effects to arise in practice, since we provided no feedback to the
subject until the payment screen was displayed at the very end of the session thus substantially restricts
opportunities for learning or strategic adjustment across rounds (see Carlsson et al., 2024 for similar
arguments). In order not to provide feedback during the trading stage, we asked participants to choose

3 Framework and hypotheses
This section formalizes how the introduction of a limit on CBDC holdings affects individuals’ resource
allocation between CBDC and bank-card holdings. We distinguish between a direct mechanical effect
of the limit and two potential indirect behavioral effects: an attraction effect and a repulsion effect.
Based on this framework, we derive testable hypotheses.

3.2 Behavioral channels
We consider two indirect behavioral effects that may arise when a holding limit is introduced: a
repulsion effect and an attraction effect. To avoid possible confounds from the direct effect of the
limit, we focus our analysis on the allocation decisions of unconstrained individuals, for whom the
limit implies no direct effect and thus no change in allocation (x lL = xlN L). Therefore, any deviation
from this benchmark reveals the presence of an indirect behavioral effect.
The repulsion effect captures a reduced interest in the restricted means of payment. When a limit
is introduced, individuals may perceive the CBDC as less attractive and reduce their allocation relative
to the No Limit condition. This implies xlL < xlN L. In contrast, the attraction effect corresponds to an
anchoring of the allocation decision to CBDC holdings towards the limit l, increasing CBDC holdings
for unconstrained individuals. This implies xlL > xlN L.
Because individuals may be subject to both effects simultaneously, we interpret an overall decrease
in CBDC holdings (x lL < xlN L) as evidence of a dominant repulsion effect, and an overall increase in
CBDC holdings (x lL > xlN L) as evidence of a dominant attraction effect. When allocations remain
unchanged, behavior is consistent with the benchmark model without indirect effects or with offsetting
attraction and repulsion forces. 14

Hypothesis 1 (Response to the limit with indirect effects) For unconstrained individuals, the
introduction of a holding limit changes CBDC allocations: xlL − xlN L= 0.

The magnitude of indirect behavioral effects is expected to depend on the level of the limit. A lower

namely those whose No Limit decisions would also leave them unconstrained under the Low limit

3.3 Reverse waterfall mechanism
We now investigate associating a reverse waterfall mechanism to the limit affects CBDC holdings. To
do so, we focus our analysis on comparisons between the Limit and the Limit & R W conditions. In
the Limit & R W condition, participants still face a limit on the number of tokens they can allocate
to CBDC holdings. However, if needed to complete the trade, one token is automatically transferred
from bank-card to CBDC holdings, provided that the individual allocated at least one token to CBDC
holdings in the allocation phase. This can have two distinct effects. First, allocating a single token

increasing the likelihood of adoption (“adoption effect”). Second, conditional on adoption, allocating
more than one token no longer provides additional transactional benefits and entails an opportunity

holdings (“intensive-margin effect”).
Hypothesis 3 (Response to the reverse waterfall mechanism) Given both the adoption and in-
tensity effects, the reverse waterfall mechanism induces individuals’ allocations to CBDC holdings to
converge toward 1: |xlL&RW − 1| < |xlL − 1|.
4 Results
We first describe the level of CBDC holdings in the No Limit condition. Then, we assess the impact of
introducing a limit by focusing on the difference between the No Limit and Limit conditions. Finally,
we investigate the impact of introducing the reverse waterfall functionality by comparing the Limit
and Limit & R W conditions. The analyses presented in this section are preregistered unless stated
otherwise.15 Finally, we briefly comment on the impact of the demographics on our main variables.

4.5 Additional analysis: individual characteristics
We explore individual determinants of i) the CBDC holdings, and ii) the change in CBDC holdings
between the No Limit and Limit conditions.
Regarding the holdings, we regress the amount allocated to CBDC holdings on a set of control
variables, first focusing only on demographics, then adding either risk aversion or variables related to
payment savviness and, finally, by including all of these variables together (seeTable A-2 in Appendix).
All regressions include country fixed-effects and heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. We find
that the more-risk averse individuals are, the more tokens they allocate to CBDC holdings. This is
consistent with bank-card holdings having a higher risk of adverse outcomes (i.e., meeting with sellers
who only accept CBDC). Male participants allocate, on average, about 0.5 less tokens to their CBDC
holdings.
We use a similar approach to study the change in CBDC holdings between the No Limit and Limit
conditions while adding as regressor CBDC holdings in the No Limit condition to control for initial
allocations (Table A-3 in Appendix). We find that individuals with a higher digital financial confidence
adjusted less their holdings. We also find that preferring cash is also associated with less adjustment.
5 Discussion and Conclusion
We study how imposing a holding limit on a means of payment affects users’ attitudes towards it. We
find that the imposition of a holding limit has both a direct mechanical effect, capping the maximum
holdings, and an indirect behavioral effect, which increases the holdings of the limited means of payment
of the participants whose initial balances were below the limit.
We interpret this outcome as due to an attraction effect of the limit: the limit acts as an anchoring
point that shifts allocations toward that value. Moreover, distinguishing between a lower and a higher
limit, we find that this increase in holdings emerges only when the limit is higher.
The asymmetry of the results under the lower and a higher limit originates from the coexistence of
two opposite indirect effects: the attraction effect described above, and a repulsion effect. The latter is
driven by the restriction of decision rights, which renders the limited means of payment less attractive.
Under the lower limit, these two effects offset each other, leaving the average allocation unchanged.

By contrast, a higher limit attenuates the repulsion effect while strengthening the attraction, thus
shifting allocations toward higher values and generating a net positive indirect effect. Indeed, we find
that, under the higher limit, the indirect effect dominates the direct effect of truncating the upper part
of the decision set, resulting in higher average holdings of the limited means of payment, and thus a
reversal of the expected effect of the limit. Finally, we provide the first empirical evidence that the
introduction of a reverse waterfall functionality can successfully mitigate the behavioral responses to
the holding limits, thereby increasing the adoption of the limited means of payment while containing
holdings. These findings shed light on indirect behavioral effects that may arise from introducing a
holding limit on a CBDC. Our experiment contrasts two means of payment: one that yields interest on
holdings but has limited acceptance, and the other that is universally accepted but unremunerated and
subject to a holding limit. In this respect, the design captures the core trade-off between remunerated
bank deposits, allowing person-to-business (P2B) payments, and an unremunerated CBDC enabling
both P2B and P2P transactions. These are expected features of, for example, the digital euro.
While caution is warranted when generalizing our results, our findings suggest that, when a limit
is set sufficiently high, it may increase CBDC holdings among individuals who, in the absence of
any constraint, would otherwise have held balances below that limit. By contrast, a sufficiently low
holding limit tends, on average, to neutralize the behavioral indirect effects. As an exploratory exercise,
we provide an order-of-magnitude interpretation of our lower and higher limit levels to enhance the
practical relevance of our results. Using a back-of-the-envelope calculation, we match quantiles of
CBDC holdings in the No Limit treatment with estimated average digital euro holdings from a euro
area–wide survey (Garcia et al., 2026). We find that the implied lower and higher limits correspond
approximately to e1000 and e5000, respectively. Indeed, in our data, 71% of participants hold no more
than 3 tokens, which matches the estimated share of individuals holding less than e1000. Similarly,
96% hold no more than 8 tokens, aligning with the estimated share of individuals holding below e5000
in the estimated real-world distribution. 26 Under the higher holding limit of e5000, extrapolating our
experimental estimates suggests an increase in CBDC holdings of about 13% for the individuals whose
unbounded holdings would be below the limit.

benefit from the payment advantages of CBDC without necessarily holding any, is a particularly useful

The views expressed are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the ECB. No 3300 / October 2026

Abstract Holding limits are a central design feature of proposed retail central bank digital currencies (CBDC). While such limits mechanically prevent individuals from exceeding a maximum balance, they may also generate behavioral responses whose directions are a priori unclear. We conducted an incentivized online experiment with participants from four euro-area countries, exogenously varying the presence and level of a holding limit to causally separate direct mechanical effects from behavioral effects. We find that behavioral responses increase holdings of the means of payment subject to the holding limit, consistent with an attraction effect. This effect is material only when the limit is high enough. Enabling reverse waterfall —automatic conversion into this limited means of payment— increases adoption while reducing holdings. These results suggest that combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms can support CBDC use while containing holdings, thereby helping to mitigate potential financial stability risks. Keywords: CBDC, holding limits, digital currency, behavioral economics, experimental economics. JEL codes: E42, C91, D14, E58. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 1

Non-technical summary Several central banks are exploring the possibility of issuing a central bank digital currency (CBDC) — a digital form of public money for everyday payments. The CBDC design needs to balance ease of use with ensuring that it preserves financial stability. In response, most CBDC projects foresee the introduction of a holding limit, which would cap the amount of CBDC that individuals could hold in their digital wallets. At the same time, automatic funding mechanisms such as the reverse waterfall functionality can allow individuals to make payments even when they do not hold sufficient CBDC, potentially reducing the need to hold large CBDC balances. While holding limits would mechanically restrict how much CBDC people can hold, they may also have a behavioral impact. For example, some individuals may view the limit as a restriction of their decision rights, decreasing the attractiveness of the CBDC. For others, instead, the limit can act as a reference point, attracting CBDC holdings towards that value. Understanding these possible responses is important to assess how much CBDC people would actually hold and thus anticipate its impact on the financial system if such limits were introduced. This paper investigates how holding limits influence individuals’ choices about how to allocate their money between different payment instruments. In particular, it studies whether the introduction of a limit changes individuals’ behavior beyond its direct mechanical effect. The analysis also provides empirical evidence on the reverse waterfall functionality. This mechanism automatically converts funds from a user’s commercial bank account into CBDC whenever the user needs to make a payment but does not currently hold enough CBDC. To disentangle the direct effect of the limit from its behavioral effects, the paper uses a controlled online experiment with 761 participants from four euro area countries: France, Germany, Italy, and Spain.

In the experiment, participants made decisions about how to allocate tokens between two means of payment, then faced automated sellers, and earned money if they held the means of payment required by the seller. One instrument bears interest but is not always accepted, while the other pays no interest, is always accepted for payments and could be subject to a holding limit. These differences capture the essence of the differences between bank-card payment and CBDC, where the former can be remunerated via a deposit account and the latter can be used for peer-to-peer payments. Our ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 2

identification strategy relies on comparing participants’ decisions in the absence and the presence of a limit, and assessing whether the level of the limit affects these behavioral responses by comparing decisions with relatively lower and higher limits. In addition, we investigate how the presence of a reverse waterfall functionality affects individuals’ responses to these limits. Our results show that holding limits can generate indirect behavioral effects. Participants whose initial holdings are below the limit, and thus would be expected to keep the same allocation in the absence of indirect effects, tend on average to increase their holdings when the limit is introduced. Moreover, distinguishing between relatively lower and higher limits, we find that this increase in holdings emerges only when the limit is higher due to an asymmetric impact of attraction and repulsion. When the limit is lower, the opposing behavioral responses offset each other, leaving average holdings unchanged. By contrast, when the limit is set at a higher level, the anchoring effect becomes stronger while the negative reaction to the restriction becomes weaker. As a result, average holdings increase after the limit is introduced with the higher limit. Finally, we find that introducing a reverse waterfall functionality both increases adoption of the limited means of payment and decreases the level of its holdings. This suggests that these kind of automated funding mechanisms can allow individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of CBDC without requiring them to hold large CBDC balances. Overall, we provide the first evidence that combining holding limits with automatic funding mech- anisms can support the use of CBDC as a means of payment while addressing concerns about potential financial stability risks. 1 Introduction Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDC) are digital forms of sovereign currency issued by the central bank. Several central banks are currently designing retail CBDC to complement physical cash by providing individuals with an additional state-backed means of payment (Illes et al., 2025). CBDC would bring central bank money into the digital age aiming to support financial inclusion, protect privacy, and make payments easier and more secure for all. They would complement banknotes and coins, giving people an additional choice about how to pay. However, preventing users from storing excessive amounts in CBDC is also important to avoid excessive outflows of deposits from banks, preserving financial stability. To address this concern, central banks such as the ECB, the Bank of England, the Bank of Canada or the People’s Bank of China are designing CBDC that would feature a “holding limit” which would limit, at any point in time, the amount of CBDC that individuals could hold in their digital wallet (Panetta, 2022; Demertzis and Mejino-L´ op ez, 2024).1 In parallel, several CBDC projects are considering automatic funding mechanisms which would allow users to make payments in CBDC without maintaining large CBDC balances. Motivated by this central feature of CBDC, this paper studies how imposing a holding limit on a means of payment affects consumers’ liquid wealth allocation. Introducing a holding limit has an obvious direct effect on individuals’ allocation decisions by preventing users from exceeding the limit. In addition to this mechanical effect, holding limits can have indirect behavioral effects reflecting a change in consumer attitudes toward the means of payment that can further affect holdings. The direction of these indirect effects is a priori not clear. On the one hand, users may perceive a means of payment associated with a holding limit as a less attractive solution, leading

them to hold fewer funds in CBDC than what is directly implied by the mechanical impact. Indeed, a limit can have an aversive impact by reducing decision rights (e.g. Bartling et al., 2014). On the other hand, the holding limit can act as a reference or anchoring point when individuals choose how much to hold, potentially leading them to hold amounts close to the limit, whereas they might have held less otherwise (e.g. Ariely et al., 2003; Abeler et al., 2011).2 Given that these effects are behavioral and real-world data on CBDC holdings are unavailable due to the lack of a large-scale CBDC implementation, we use an 1Beyond CBDC, holding limits have also been considered for stablecoins (Bank of England, 2025). 2Furnham and Boo (2011) provide a literature review showing that the anchoring effect is one of the most robust cognitive heuristics. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 4

experimental approach to assess whether indirect effects occur and, if so, to identify the direction of their influence on holdings. Despite the importance of understanding the impact of a holding limit on CBDC holdings, to date, there is no paper explicitly dedicated to this question. Incentivized experiments on CBDC have focused on different aspects of the introduction of a CBDC on individuals’ portfolio allocations including the introduction of a new payment method (Arifovic et al., 2023), greater privacy compared with other digital payment instruments (Borgonovo et al., 2021; Magin et al., 2026), the possibility of bearing interest (Camera, 2024), and their digital nature relative to cash (Camera et al., 2016).3 However, they do not address the role of the holding limit. 4 More closely related to our contribution, some studies use surveys, which include questions on holding limits but do not experimentally manipulate either the existence or the level of such limits. For example, van der Horst and van Gent (2025) conduct a survey experiment on digital euro and find that, on average, participants consider e1,297 to be a logical amount for a holding limit by directly asking for the amounts to participants. Bidder et al. (2024) develop a quantitative macroeconomic model calibrated using survey data and show that the introduction of a holding limit is a necessary condition for a CBDC to be welfare-improving. Even closer to our study, Georgarakos et al. (2025) estimate in a survey experiment the causal effect of holding limits ranging from e1000 to e120000 on the propensity to adopt the digital euro and the amount allocated to it compared with other liquid assets. They find that higher holding limits tend to increase amount allocated. Our preregistered study contributes to the literature by causally assessing the overall impact of the introduction of a holding limit

on individuals’ portfolio allocation while disentangling its direct mechanical effect from its indirect behavioral effects. To achieve this objective, we employ an online incentivized experiment that exogenously varies both the presence and the level of a holding limit. Specifically, participants face an allocation decision between two means of payment, first without any holding limit, and subsequently with one means subject to a holding limit. The baseline (No Limit ) condition allows us to elicit individual behavior in the absence of constraints, which can then be compared to the behavior under the imposition of a holding limit to identify causal effects. After the 3See Jiang (2020) for a comprehensive review of experiments on CBDC. 4A growing literature (Li, 2023; Lambert et al., 2024; Nocciola and Zamora-P´ erez,2024) also aims to quantify the potential CBDC demand, which is a key variable to determine the economic and financial stability implications of its introduction, using econometric techniques and counterfactual exercises. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 5

allocation choice, participants use allocated tokens in trading activities that generate monetary payoffs. Our experimental design differentiates itself from previous survey-based experiments by incorporating real monetary incentives, thereby mitigating potential biases commonly found in survey studies (e.g., social desirability bias, hypothetical bias, etc.; Camerer and Hogarth , 1999). In addition, we investigate how the presence of a reverse waterfall functionality affects individuals’ responses to these limits. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study how individuals respond to a CBDC associated with a reverse waterfall (R W) functionality, a key feature designed to preserve CBDC usability while limiting holdings in, for example, the foreseen design of the digital euro (ECB, 2024b).5 This functionality enables users to draw on funds from a linked commercial bank deposit account automatically converting them into CBDC whenever the user’s CBDC balance is insufficient to complete a payment. This functionality is designed to operate alongside holding limits, allowing policymakers to constrain CBDC holdings without restricting the use of CBDC as a means of payment. However, little is known empirically about how individuals would respond to such a feature or about its effect on CBDC holdings. To address this gap, our experimental design includes a final condition in which the reverse waterfall functionality is enabled in the presence of a holding limit. Our subject pool consists of 761 individuals from the four most populous euro area countries— France, Germany, Italy, and Spain—, all recruited via the online research platform Prolific. Sampling potential future users of the digital euro across multiple countries enhances the external validity of our findings for the euro area. 6 Our results highlight that holding limits can generate indirect behavioral effects, beyond their mechanical role of capping maximum holdings. We find evidence of two opposing mechanisms affecting the holdings of

a substantial fraction of “unconstrained” individuals (i.e., those whose initial CBDC holdings were below the limit). About 37% of them either increase (“attraction effect”) or decrease (“repulsion effect”) their CBDC holdings once the limit is introduced and these effects cannot be attributed to the mechanical impact of the limit. The overall net change thus depends on the relative strength of each indirect effect, which appears to depend on the level at which the limit is set. Under the 5The term “reverse” is used to distinguish this mechanism from the “waterfall” functionality, which operates in the opposite direction: CBDC is automatically transferred to bank deposits when incoming transfers cause holdings to exceed the holding limit. 6The selection of these four countries reflects a trade-off between broad population coverage, as they account for more than half of the euro area’s population, and practical constraints related to translating materials into multiple native languages and the depth of available participant pools on Prolific. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 6

lower limit, attraction and repulsion offset each other, leaving the average holdings of the unconstrained individuals unaffected. Under the higher limit, the repulsion effect is attenuated while the attraction effect is strengthened, leading to a net increase in holdings of the limited means of payment among unconstrained participants. Strikingly, when the limit is relatively high, the indirect behavioral effect dominates the direct mechanical effect, resulting in higher average holdings of the limited means of payment in the whole sample. Finally, we show that introducing a reverse waterfall functionality increases adoption while reducing average holdings. Thus, the waterfall can allow individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of CBDC without requiring them to hold large CBDC balances. Taken together, these results highlight the potential value of combining holding limits with automatic funding mechanisms to support CBDC use while containing CBDC holdings. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: section 2 presents the experimental design, section 3 reports the theoretical framework and hypotheses, section 4 presents the results and section 5 concludes. 2 Experimental Design In our experiment, participants first allocate their tokens between two means of payment, then they face automated sellers with whom they aim to complete trades. One means of payment, bank-card, yields interests but is rejected by some sellers while the other one, CBDC, is universally accepted but non-remunerated.7 The experiment follows a 3 × 2 design varying the presence of a limit and its level. 2.1 Characteristics of the means of payment The characteristics of the two payment methods draw inspiration from key features of bank-card and CBDC payments. However, they are not intended to replicate these payment methods in full detail, but to introduce stylized comparative advantages to capture their essential characteristics while main- taining a simplified structure that facilitates the understanding of the

participants. Tokens allocated 7While neutral phrasing was used in the experiment presenting the two means of payment as payment A and payment B, we refer to them using the name of the real-world instruments that inspired them. Accordingly, the remunerated means is referred to as “bank-card” and the other one as “CBDC”. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 7

Thus, this reflects the opposition between a non-interest bearing CBDC, such as the one envisaged in the euro area (ECB, 2025), and remunerated bank deposits. Bank-card payments are only accepted by 90% of the sellers in the market, capturing the limited ability to make peer-to-peer (P2P) bank-card payments. By contrast, CBDC payments are accepted by all sellers reflecting the possibility to do P2P payments and legal tender status as envisaged, for example, by the digital-euro design. 8 Furthermore, participants incur an entry cost of 0.5 tokens to allocate at least 1 token to their CBDC holdings, capturing the cost of transitioning to a new means of payment as captured by, for example, Arifovic et al. (2023) and Magin et al. (2026). 2.2 Stages, treatments and conditions The experiment is composed of three conditions and two treatments. Each condition consists of two stages: an allocation stage and a trading stage. Allocation stage: Participants face an allocation decision in which they need to allocate their endowment of 10 tokens between the two payment methods. Trading stage: After their allocation decision, participants face 10 sellers with whom they can “trade” in 10 successive rounds. Participants are incentivized to realize successful trades. 11 Require- ments needed for a trade to be successful are varied between conditions. Condition variations: As mentioned earlier, each participant faces three conditions during the experiment (see Figure 1). In the No Limit condition, there is no limit on the number of tokens they can allocate to their bank-card holdings. In the Limit and Limit & R W conditions, the number of tokens that can be allocated to CBDC holdings is capped (the ceiling is varied between treatments). In addition, the Limit & R W condition differs from the other two as regards the outcome of a trade with a seller accepting only CBDC if the participant does not have tokens allocated to CBDC when meeting the seller. In the No Limit and Limit, this trade fails. By contrast, in the Limit & R W condition a token is automatically transferred from bank to CBDC holdings and is used to complete the trade, providing that the participant has allocated at least one token to CBDC holdings in the allocation phase. This latter constraint captures the need to have a CBDC account open to use the reverse waterfall mechanism. Figure 1: Bet ween-subjects treatments and within-subjects conditions 2.3 Experimen tal procedures The experiment was conducted online using the platform Prolific in November 2025. A total of 761 individuals participated from the four most populated euro area countries, namely France, Germany, Italy, and Spain (190 participants per country except 191 for Spain; 374 in the Low Limit treatment and 387 in the High Limit treatment). Instructions were provided in the native language of each country (see English translation in Appendix E). The average age of the participants was 35 years old (sd = 11) and 49.6% were female. One condition, among the 3 conditions, was randomly selected for the payment. Each successful trade yielded 10 points and points were converted at a rate of 50 points per £1.12 The bonus payment was on average equal to £1.98. It adds to the hourly average payment of £2 (median time of 13 minutes) to constitute the total payoff per subject. All participants faced the conditions in the same order: No Limit, Limit and Limit & R W. We chose to position the No Limit condition first in order to have a benchmark allocation where the potential implementation of a limit was unknown to the subject. Indeed, withdrawing the limit could have affected allocations in a No Limit condition presented second thus preventing a clean estimation of the impact of introducing a limit. Although this choice may introduce a potential order effect, the design leaves little room for such effects to arise in practice, since we provided no feedback to the subject until the payment screen was displayed at the very end of the session thus substantially restricts opportunities for learning or strategic adjustment across rounds (see Carlsson et al., 2024 for similar arguments). In order not to provide feedback during the trading
stage, we asked participants to choose 12While all pa rticipants were from euro area countries, the experiment utilized Prolific’s default currency. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 10

which means of payment to use if the seller accepted both means of payment and they had both types of tokens available in conditions No Limit and Limit. This decision was then applied for all potential transactions.13 In the Limit & R W, this decision was actually irrelevant as participants either: i) allocated at least one token to CBDC and could complete all trades, ii) allocated all their tokens to card-payment and thus could only pay with card, if accepted by the seller. At the end of the experiment, participants were asked to report their age, gender, native language as well as their self-reported risk preferences (Dohmen et al.,2011). We also elicited how confident they are in their ability to manage their finances using digital tools (such as online banking apps, digital wallets, or investment platforms) and their preferred payment methods when paying for goods or services in person (e.g., in stores) among cash, debit or credit card, a mobile payment app, or a digital wallet (the exact instructions are reported in Appendix E). Finally, participants could rate the clarity of the instructions and explain their allocation choices in each condition (open-ended non-mandatory questions). 3 Framework and hypotheses This section formalizes how the introduction of a limit on CBDC holdings affects individuals’ resource allocation between CBDC and bank-card holdings. We distinguish between a direct mechanical effect of the limit and two potential indirect behavioral effects: an attraction effect and a repulsion effect. Based on this framework, we derive testable hypotheses. 3.1 Setup Let xlC ∈ {0, . . . ,10} denote the number of tokens allocated to CBDC holdings by an individual in condition C ∈ {N L, L, L&RW} and treatment with a

When a limit is introduced, individuals may perceive the CBDC as less attractive and reduce their allocation relative to the No Limit condition. This implies xlL < xlN L. In contrast, the attraction effect corresponds to an anchoring of the allocation decision to CBDC holdings towards the limit l, increasing CBDC holdings for unconstrained individuals. Hypothesis 1 (Response to the limit with indirect effects) For unconstrained individuals, the introduction of a holding limit changes CBDC allocations: xlL − xlN L= 0. A negative change indicates a dominant repulsion effect, a positive change indicates a dominant at- traction effect, while no change is consistent both with offsetting attraction and repulsion forces or no indirect effects. The magnitude of indirect behavioral effects is expected to depend on the level of the limit. A lower limit restricts decision rights more strongly and is therefore expected to generate stronger repulsion effects. By contrast, a higher limit provides a higher salient anchor and is expected to generate stronger attraction effects. We also find that preferring cash is also associated with less adjustment. 5 Discussion and Conclusion We study how imposing a holding limit on a means of payment affects users’ attitudes towards it. We find that the imposition of a holding limit has both a direct mechanical effect, capping the maximum holdings, and an indirect behavioral effect, which increases the holdings of the limited means of payment of the participants whose initial balances were below the limit. We interpret this outcome as due to an attraction effect of the limit: the limit acts as an anchoring point that shifts allocations toward that value. Moreover, distinguishing between a lower and a higher limit, we find

that this increase in holdings emerges only when the limit is higher. The asymmetry of the results under the lower and a higher limit originates from the coexistence of two opposite indirect effects: the attraction effect described above, and a repulsion effect. The latter is driven by the restriction of decision rights, which renders the limited means of payment less attractive. Under the lower limit, these two effects offset each other, leaving the average allocation unchanged. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 21

By contrast, a higher limit attenuates the repulsion effect while strengthening the attraction, thus shifting allocations toward higher values and generating a net positive indirect effect. Indeed, we find that, under the higher limit, the indirect effect dominates the direct effect of truncating the upper part of the decision set, resulting in higher average holdings of the limited means of payment, and thus a reversal of the expected effect of the limit. Finally, we provide the first empirical evidence that the introduction of a reverse waterfall functionality can successfully mitigate the behavioral responses to the holding limits, thereby increasing the adoption of the limited means of payment while containing holdings. These findings shed light on indirect behavioral effects that may arise from introducing a holding limit on a CBDC. Our experiment contrasts two means of payment: one that yields interest on holdings but has limited acceptance, and the other that is universally accepted but unremunerated and subject to a holding limit. In this respect, the design captures the core trade-off between remunerated bank deposits, allowing person-to-business (P2B) payments, and an unremunerated CBDC enabling both P2B and P2P transactions. These are expected features of, for example, the digital euro. While caution is warranted when generalizing our results, our findings suggest that, when a limit is set sufficiently high, it may increase CBDC holdings among individuals who, in the absence of any constraint, would otherwise have held balances below that limit. By contrast, a sufficiently low holding limit tends, on average, to neutralize the behavioral indirect effects. As an exploratory exercise, we provide an order-of-magnitude interpretation of our lower and higher limit levels to enhance the practical relevance of our results. Using a back-of-the-envelope calculation, we match quantiles of CBDC holdings in the No Limit treatment with estimated average digital euro holdings

from a euro area–wide survey (Garcia et al., 2026). We find that the implied lower and higher limits correspond approximately to e1000 and e5000, respectively. Indeed, in our data, 71% of participants hold no more than 3 tokens, which matches the estimated share of individuals holding less than e1000. Similarly, 96% hold no more than 8 tokens, aligning with the estimated share of individuals holding below e5000 in the estimated real-world distribution. 26 Under the higher holding limit of e5000, extrapolating our experimental estimates suggests an increase in CBDC holdings of about 13% for the individuals whose unbounded holdings would be below the limit. 26This correspondence is consistent with Kim et al. (2025) that estimate that, in South Korea, less than 7% of individuals would be constrained with a holding limit equivalent to e3000. In our experiment, 6.5% of the participants are constrained by a limit of 6 tokens. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 22

Our resul ts further suggest that the reverse waterfall functionality, which allows individuals to benefit from the payment advantages of CBDC without necessarily holding any, is a particularly useful policy tool. Setting the level of the holding limit primarily reflects a trade-off between usability and financial stability: a higher limit enhances usability by allowing larger holdings, while a lower limit reduces the potential impact on the banking sector by limiting CBDC holdings and, therefore, possible deposit outflows from commercial banks. When used in combination with a holding limit, a reverse waterfall mechanism increases CBDC adoption while simultaneously reducing average holdings, thereby delivering gains on both sides of the usability–financial stability trade-off. We first compute the optimal strategy provided that a digital euro account is open ( x >0). The payoff raised by tokens allocated to CBDC is unchanged. D Robustness b y country In this section, we assess the robustness of our results by examining each country separately. We first discuss the direction and magnitude of the effects by country, and then turn to their statistical significance. Regarding Result 1, the difference in CBDC holdings between the Limit and No Limit conditions for unconstrained participants is, in every country, consistent with the direction reported in Result 1. The magnitude of this difference ranges from 0.16 in Italy to 0.23 in Spain, compared with a sample- wide average of 0.19. Similarly, for Result 2, the difference between the High Limit and Low Limit treatments in the change in CBDC holdings between the Limit and No Limit conditions of ex-ante similar unconstrained participants is positive in all countries, thereby confirming Result 2 at the country level. This effect varies from 0.26 in France to 0.59 in Germany, relative to a sample average of 0.41. Finally, consistent with Result 3, the difference in CBDC holdings between the Limit & R W and Limit conditions is negative in all countries. The magnitude of this effect ranges from -0.34 in Spain to -0.69 in France, compared with a sample average of -0.43. Statistical significance at the country level is naturally affected by the fourfold reduction in sample size relative to the pooled analysis, which limits the power of country-specific tests. For Result 1, p-values of Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing holdings in the No Limit and Limit conditions are between 0.06 and 0.38. For Result 2, p-values of Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing change in holdings of unconstrained participants for the High Limit treatment and 0 are between 0.05 and 0.51. Finally for Result 3, the Wilcoxon signed-rank tests comparing absolute deviation from 1 in Limit and Limit & R W conditions have p-value of

at most 0.002. As an answer to the lack of power, we complement previous analysis with tests on whether country-level effects differ from the overall effect using Mann-Whitney tests. For Result 1, we find no statistically significant differences at conventional significance levels (ES, p-value = 0.75; FR, p-value = 0.87; IT, p-value = 0.70 and DE, p-value = 0.59). The same holds for Result 2 (ES, p-value = 0.96; FR, p-value = 0.45; IT, p-value = 0.99 and DE, p-value = 0.38) and Result 3 (ES, p-value = 0.35; FR, p-value = 0.11; IT, p-value = 0.68 and DE, p-value = 0.81). In conclusion, we find that country-level effect sizes are always in the same direction as the sample- ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 32

ave rage effects. Using statistical tests that suffer from low power, we find that while effects are not always statistically significant at the country level, they are also never statistically different from the sample-average effects. We thus conclude that the evidence points toward the robustness of our results at the country level. ECB Working Paper Series No 3300 33
